claim: Parkinson's disease affects over 6 million people worldwide.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects over 6 million people worldwide, representing the second most common neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is a factual statement about PD prevalence that is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Parkinson's disease represents the second most common neurodegenerative disease.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects over 6 million people worldwide, representing the second most common neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about PD's prevalence among neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Parkinson's disease places a burden measured in hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
source: PD is slowly progressing and typically leads to years of aggravating disability, thereby placing a huge burden on families, health care systems, and society, measured in hundreds of billions of dollars annually (Olesen et al., 2012; Obeso et al., 2017; Przedborski, 2017; Bloem et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Patients with Parkinson's disease display progressive loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Patients with PD display a diverse set of motor and non-motor symptoms with an underlying progressive loss of midbrain dopaminergic neurons (Schapira, 2009; Schapira et al., 2017; Bloem et al., 2021), mechanisms of which are widely studied in animal models of the disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Most successful rodent models of Parkinson's disease are toxin-based.
source: Unlike the genetic mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, most of the successful rodent models of PD are also toxin-based, making it difficult to exploit and further our understanding of the genetic bases of the disease (Cannon and Greenamyre, 2010; Bové and Perier, 2012; Breger and Fuzzati Armentero, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in the PARK2 gene are associated with autosomal-recessive forms of Parkinson's disease.
source: Notably, mutations in the PARK2 gene, which encodes the Parkin protein involved in maintaining mitochondrial integrity, are associated with autosomal-recessive forms of PD (Guo, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Parkin loss-of-function mutant flies have advanced mitochondrial aging and structural mitochondrial damage.
source: Parkin loss-of-function mutant flies were found to have advanced mitochondrial aging, structural mitochondrial damage, and a consequential selective loss of dopaminergic neurons (Cackovic et al., 2018), leading to motor deficits assessed by a climbing assay (Chambers et al., 2013; Cackovic et al., 2018), as well as non-motor PD phenotypes including memory deficits (Julienne et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mutations in the SNCA gene of α-Synuclein are associated with familial forms of Parkinson's disease.
source: Mutations in the SNCA gene of α-Synuclein (α-Syn) are also associated with familial forms of PD (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997) and α-Syn has been shown to accumulate in Lewy bodies and neurites (Spillantini et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: α-Synuclein accumulates in Lewy bodies and neurites.
source: Mutations in the SNCA gene of α-Synuclein (α-Syn) are also associated with familial forms of PD (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997) and α-Syn has been shown to accumulate in Lewy bodies and neurites (Spillantini et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: α-Synuclein proteins are found in pre-synaptic terminals in humans and mice.
source: α-Syn proteins have been found in the pre-synaptic terminals in humans and mice (Kahle et al., 2000) and are thought to be involved in regulating dopamine (DA) synthesis under physiological conditions by reducing tyrosine hydroxylase activity (Perez et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Expression of human α-Synuclein in flies shows age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons and locomotor dysfunction.
source: Expression of human α-Syn in flies has been proposed as a genetic model of PD, showing age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons and locomotor dysfunction in a climbing assay (Feany and Bender, 2000; Haywood and Staveley, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Some studies found normal locomotion and dopaminergic cell counts in flies expressing human α-Synuclein.
source: However, other studies found normal locomotion and dopaminergic cell counts in these flies, casting doubts on the validity of this model (Pesah et al., 2005; Nagoshi, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The D1-like dopamine receptor mediates ethanol-induced locomotion in the ellipsoid body.
source: Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated that the D1-like DA receptor mediates ethanol-induced locomotion in the ellipsoid body (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Dop1R1 is involved in turning behavior for goal-directed locomotion.
source: Furthermore, Dop1R1 has been shown to be involved in turning behavior for goal-directed locomotion (Kottler et al., 2019) and startle-induced negative geotaxis (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Dop1R1 is involved in startle-induced negative geotaxis.
source: Furthermore, Dop1R1 has been shown to be involved in turning behavior for goal-directed locomotion (Kottler et al., 2019) and startle-induced negative geotaxis (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Flies expressing the R275W mutant allele of human Parkin showed slower average locomotion speed.
source: We found that flies expressing the R275W mutant allele of human Parkin ('Parkin flies') showed slower average locomotion speed, which, in contrast, was not a characteristic of flies expressing the A53T mutant allele of the human SNCA gene ('α-Syn flies').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Flies expressing the A53T mutant allele of human SNCA gene did not show slower average locomotion speed.
source: We found that flies expressing the R275W mutant allele of human Parkin ('Parkin flies') showed slower average locomotion speed, which, in contrast, was not a characteristic of flies expressing the A53T mutant allele of the human SNCA gene ('α-Syn flies').
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Parkin flies showed less behavioral reactivity to passing shadows compared to controls.
source: Parkin flies also showed less behavioral reactivity to passing shadows compared to controls, whereas α-Syn flies showed increased durations of stopping after the stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: α-Synuclein flies showed increased durations of stopping after shadow stimuli.
source: Parkin flies also showed less behavioral reactivity to passing shadows compared to controls, whereas α-Syn flies showed increased durations of stopping after the stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Dopamine receptor mutant flies showed reduced speed and less behavioral reactivity similar to Parkin flies.
source: Dopamine receptor mutant flies showed reduced speed and less behavioral reactivity similar to Parkin flies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Dop1R1 mutant flies exhibited more pronounced behavioral alterations than the other two receptor mutants in most parameters tested.
source: Dop1R1 mutant flies exhibited more pronounced behavioral alterations than the other two receptor mutants in most of the parameters tested.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The behavioral apparatus features 13 tunnels for simultaneous tracking of 13 individual flies.
source: To do this, we designed a transparent plexiglass arena (Figure 1a), featuring 13 tunnels (53 mm x 5 mm) for simultaneous tracking of 13 individual flies.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the study, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: The height of the tunnels was designed to allow free walking in two dimensions but prevent jumps and flight.
source: The height of the tunnels (1.5 mm) was designed to allow free walking in two dimensions but prevent jumps and flight.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed three main stereotypical behavioral responses across flies in addition to trials where no significant response was evoked.
source: This analysis consistently revealed three main stereotypical behavioral responses across flies in addition to the trials where no significant response was evoked (Figure 2b).
evidence: This describes the results of data analysis with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Fruit flies were restricted to choose among freezing, slowing, and running since jumping and flying were not possible in the arena.
source: Since jumping and flying were not possible in the arena, fruit flies were restricted to choose among freezing, slowing (also observed in Zacarias et al., 2018), and running.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and is also supported by a citation.

claim: Parkin flies showed reduced mean speed compared to iso w1118 controls (24.96% reduction, p=6.55 × 10–6).
source: We found that Parkin flies showed reduced mean speed compared to controls which expressed the Gal4 driver alone (24.96% reduction, p=6.55 × 10–6, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3a, top), while α-Syn flies did not show significant reduction (p=0.799, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: α-Synuclein flies did not show significant reduction in mean speed compared to controls (p=0.799).
source: We found that Parkin flies showed reduced mean speed compared to controls which expressed the Gal4 driver alone (24.96% reduction, p=6.55 × 10–6, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3a, top), while α-Syn flies did not show significant reduction (p=0.799, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R1 mutant flies showed 19.68% decrease in mean speed compared to y1 w67c2 controls (p=0.0016).
source: We observed similar changes in dopamine receptor mutant flies, where the Dop1R1 and DopEcR defective lines showed a robust mean speed decrease compared to the control groups (Dop1R1, 19.68% decrease compared to y1 w67c2, p=0.0016; DopEcR, 32.97% decrease compared to w1118, p=0.0034; Figure 3a, bottom), while the Dop1R2 mutant flies only showed a non-significant speed decrease (21.73% compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.1009, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: DopEcR mutant flies showed 32.97% decrease in mean speed compared to w1118 controls (p=0.0034).
source: We observed similar changes in dopamine receptor mutant flies, where the Dop1R1 and DopEcR defective lines showed a robust mean speed decrease compared to the control groups (Dop1R1, 19.68% decrease compared to y1 w67c2, p=0.0016; DopEcR, 32.97% decrease compared to w1118, p=0.0034; Figure 3a, bottom), while the Dop1R2 mutant flies only showed a non-significant speed decrease (21.73% compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.1009, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R2 mutant flies showed a non-significant speed decrease (21.73% compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.1009).
source: We observed similar changes in dopamine receptor mutant flies, where the Dop1R1 and DopEcR defective lines showed a robust mean speed decrease compared to the control groups (Dop1R1, 19.68% decrease compared to y1 w67c2, p=0.0016; DopEcR, 32.97% decrease compared to w1118, p=0.0034; Figure 3a, bottom), while the Dop1R2 mutant flies only showed a non-significant speed decrease (21.73% compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.1009, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Parkin flies froze after stimuli less frequently, stopping in 37.72% of trials compared to 43.48% in iso w1118 animals (p=0.0043).
source: We found that PD model flies showed line-specific alterations in their freezing behavior. Parkin flies froze after stimuli less frequently, stopping in 37.72% of trials compared to the 43.48% observed in the iso w1118 animals (p=0.0043, Mann Whitney U-test; Figure 3b, top).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Parkin flies showed normal duration of pauses in locomotion in stop trials (p=0.8018 compared to iso w1118).
source: However, in the stop trials, they showed normal duration of pauses in locomotion (p=0.8018 compared to iso w1118, Mann Whitney U-test; Figure 3c, top).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: α-Synuclein flies showed an unchanged stopping frequency compared to controls (p=0.0768 compared to iso w1118).
source: In contrast, α-Syn flies showed an unchanged stopping frequency when compared to controls (p=0.0768 compared to iso w1118, Mann-Whitney U-test), but their stop durations showed a large increase (116.98% increase compared to iso w1118, p=2.18 × 10–11, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: α-Synuclein flies showed a 116.98% increase in stop durations compared to iso w1118 (p=2.18 × 10–11).
source: In contrast, α-Syn flies showed an unchanged stopping frequency when compared to controls (p=0.0768 compared to iso w1118, Mann-Whitney U-test), but their stop durations showed a large increase (116.98% increase compared to iso w1118, p=2.18 × 10–11, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dopamine receptor mutant flies did not show significant differences in their freezing behavior relative to controls.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to PD model flies, dopamine receptor mutant flies did not show significant differences in their freezing behavior relative to controls (stop proportion: Dop1R1, p=0.0631 compared to y1 w67c23; Dop1R2, p=0.1838 compared to y1 w67c23; DopEcR, p=0.1445 compared to w1118; Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3b, bottom; stop duration: Dop1R1, p=0.893 compared to y1 w67c23; Dop1R2, p=0.154 compared to y1 w67c23; DopEcR, p=0.3576 compared to w1118; Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3c, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: α-Synuclein flies showed a reduced aptitude to increase their speed upon encountering threatening stimuli (26.67% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=8.4 × 10–6).
source: α-Syn flies showed a reduced aptitude to increase their speed, or 'run', upon encountering threatening stimuli (26.67% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=8.4 × 10–6, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3d, top).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R1 mutant flies showed 25% decrease in speed-up behavior compared to y1 w67c23 (p=0.0122).
source: Similar results were found in Dop1R1 (25% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0122; Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3d, bottom) and Dop1R2 (41.67% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0024, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not in DopEcR mutant flies (compared to w1118, p=0.6598, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R2 mutant flies showed 41.67% decrease in speed-up behavior compared to y1 w67c23 (p=0.0024).
source: Similar results were found in Dop1R1 (25% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0122; Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3d, bottom) and Dop1R2 (41.67% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0024, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not in DopEcR mutant flies (compared to w1118, p=0.6598, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: DopEcR mutant flies did not show significant decrease in speed-up behavior compared to w1118 (p=0.6598).
source: Similar results were found in Dop1R1 (25% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0122; Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3d, bottom) and Dop1R2 (41.67% decrease compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0024, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not in DopEcR mutant flies (compared to w1118, p=0.6598, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Frequency of slowing was moderately decreased in Parkin flies (14.38% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.0723).
source: Frequency of slowing, that is reducing their speed without freezing in a full stop, was moderately decreased in Parkin (14.38% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.0723, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3e, top) and DopEcR mutant flies (15.28% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.020, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3e, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Frequency of slowing was decreased in DopEcR mutant flies (15.28% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.020).
source: Frequency of slowing, that is reducing their speed without freezing in a full stop, was moderately decreased in Parkin (14.38% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.0723, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3e, top) and DopEcR mutant flies (15.28% decrease compared to iso w1118, p=0.020, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 3e, bottom).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: All mutations tested resulted in decreased reactivity to threatening stimuli.
source: Overall, all mutations tested resulted in decreased reactivity to threatening stimuli, confirmed by a significant increase in the proportion of trials where no reactions were detected (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Parkin flies showed 30% increase in no-reaction trials compared to iso w1118 (p=0.0043).
source: This effect was significant for Parkin flies (30% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0043, Mann-Whitney U-test), as well as for Dop1R1 (50% increase compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0173, Mann-Whitney U-test) and DopEcR mutant flies (50% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0167, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not for α-Syn (α-Syn vs. iso w1118, p=0.151, Mann-Whitney U-test) and Dop1R2 mutant flies (Dop1R2 vs. y1 w67c23, p=0.1903, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R1 mutant flies showed 50% increase in no-reaction trials compared to y1 w67c23 (p=0.0173).
source: This effect was significant for Parkin flies (30% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0043, Mann-Whitney U-test), as well as for Dop1R1 (50% increase compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0173, Mann-Whitney U-test) and DopEcR mutant flies (50% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0167, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not for α-Syn (α-Syn vs. iso w1118, p=0.151, Mann-Whitney U-test) and Dop1R2 mutant flies (Dop1R2 vs. y1 w67c23, p=0.1903, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: DopEcR mutant flies showed 50% increase in no-reaction trials compared to iso w1118 (p=0.0167).
source: This effect was significant for Parkin flies (30% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0043, Mann-Whitney U-test), as well as for Dop1R1 (50% increase compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0173, Mann-Whitney U-test) and DopEcR mutant flies (50% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0167, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not for α-Syn (α-Syn vs. iso w1118, p=0.151, Mann-Whitney U-test) and Dop1R2 mutant flies (Dop1R2 vs. y1 w67c23, p=0.1903, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: α-Synuclein flies did not show significant increase in no-reaction trials compared to iso w1118 (p=0.151).
source: This effect was significant for Parkin flies (30% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0043, Mann-Whitney U-test), as well as for Dop1R1 (50% increase compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0173, Mann-Whitney U-test) and DopEcR mutant flies (50% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0167, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not for α-Syn (α-Syn vs. iso w1118, p=0.151, Mann-Whitney U-test) and Dop1R2 mutant flies (Dop1R2 vs. y1 w67c23, p=0.1903, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dop1R2 mutant flies did not show significant increase in no-reaction trials compared to y1 w67c23 (p=0.1903).
source: This effect was significant for Parkin flies (30% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0043, Mann-Whitney U-test), as well as for Dop1R1 (50% increase compared to y1 w67c23, p=0.0173, Mann-Whitney U-test) and DopEcR mutant flies (50% increase compared to iso w1118, p=0.0167, Mann-Whitney U-test), but not for α-Syn (α-Syn vs. iso w1118, p=0.151, Mann-Whitney U-test) and Dop1R2 mutant flies (Dop1R2 vs. y1 w67c23, p=0.1903, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Results from NP6510-Gal4 and TH-Gal4 lines were largely similar to those of the Ddc-Gal4 lines.
source: Results from these tests were largely similar to those of the Ddc-Gal4 lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), reproducing the decreased speed (NP6510-Gal4-R275W, 30.3% decrease compared to NP6510-Gal4- iso w1118, p=1.55 x 10–6; NP6510-Gal4-A53T, 20.4% decrease compared to NP6510-Gal4- iso w1118, p=5.82 x 10–10; TH-Gal4-R275W, 13.08% decrease compared to TH-Gal4- iso w1118, p=1.49 x 10–6; TH-Gal4-A53T, 17.57% decrease compared to TH-Gal4- iso w1118, p=6.75 x 10–7; Mann–Whitney U-test) and decreased overall reactivity (NP6510-Gal4-R275W, 57.14% increase in 'No reaction' compared to NP6510-Gal4- iso w1118, p=3.49–8; NP6510-Gal4-A53T, 14.28% increase in 'No reaction' compared to NP6510-Gal4- iso w1118, p=0.1658; TH-Gal4-R275W, 66.7% increase in 'No reaction' compared to TH-Gal4- iso w1118, p=2.77 x 10–10; TH-Gal4-A53T, 66.7% increase in 'No reaction' compared to TH-Gal4- iso w1118, p=1.11 x 10–6; Mann–Whitney U-test) of PD-model flies.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Mutations in dopaminergic neurons alone were sufficient to produce the phenotypical changes observed.
source: Overall, this suggests that mutations in the dopaminergic neurons alone were sufficient to produce the above-described phenotypical changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of different Gal4 driver lines.

claim: Stop duration showed a significantly larger dispersion in α-Synuclein flies compared to controls (p=0.0001).
source: We found that stop duration showed a significantly larger dispersion in α-Syn flies compared to controls (p=0.0001, permutation test; Figure 3—figure supplement 3), while no other significant difference in data variance was detected.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: No significant difference between groups was observed in their speed-behavioral response relationship for any of the response types.
source: We did not observe a significant difference between groups in their speed - behavioral response relationship for any of the response types (stops, p=0.4226; slow down, p=0.6025; speed up, p=0.9074; no reaction p=0.4692; two-way ANOVA genotype × speed interaction).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Differences in baseline speed alone did not explain the observed differences in behavioral reactions.
source: In most of the groups, we found a significant difference between the predicted and the measured response type distributions, suggesting a role for other behavioral differences among the mutant lines beyond the baseline speed differences (Parkin, p=0.0487; α-Syn, p<0.000001; Dop1R1, p=0.332; Dop1R2, p=0.006157; DopEcR, p=0.003901, chi-square test).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's simulation analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The behavior of 1-day-old flies was significantly different from all other age groups.
source: Our data showed that the behavior of 1-day-old flies was significantly different from all other age groups.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's age-group comparison experiments.

claim: One-day-old flies stopped significantly more often, and the frequency of stopping gradually decreased with age in all groups.
source: One-day-old flies stopped significantly more often, and the frequency of stopping gradually decreased with age in all groups (two-way ANOVA, age, p=1.87 x 10–20, f=26.11; genotype, p=1.3 x 10–29, f=38.42; genotype ×age, p=3.18 x 10–6, f=3.54; 1-day-old vs. 1-week-old, p=1.1 x 10–4; 1-week-old vs. 2-week-old, p=0.0074, 2-week-old vs. 3-week-old, p=0.1015; 3-week-old vs. 4-week-old, p=0.0079, Mann-Whitney test for post hoc analysis).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The probability of slowing down showed a substantial increase from 1-day-old to 1-week-old animals, and then remained relatively stable until the 4th week.
source: In contrast, the probability of slowing down showed a substantial increase from 1-day-old to 1-week-old animals, and then remained relatively stable until the 4th week (two-way ANOVA, age, p=9.11 x 10–15, f=18.72; genotype, p=1.4 x 10–21, f=27.59; genotype ×age, p=0.0028, f=2.291; 1-day-old vs. 1-week-old, p=5.9 x 10–10; 1-week-old vs. 2-week-old, p=0.992; 2-week-old vs. 3-week-old, p=0.0305; 3-week-old vs. 4-week-old, p=0.033; Mann-Whitney test for post hoc analysis).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: The 4-week-old animals showed a significant decrease in speeding up compared to 3-week-old flies.
source: The probability of speeding up showed a similar trend, except that the 4-week-old animals showed a significant decrease compared to 3-week-old flies (two-way ANOVA, age, p=2.48 x 10–15, f=19.44; genotype, p=2.28 x 10–44, f=59.48; genotype ×age, p=1.1 x 10–7, f=4.12; 1-day-old vs 1-week-old, p=2.64 x 10–10; 1-week-old vs. 2-week-old, p=0.572; 2-week-old vs. 3-week-old, p=0.3445; 3-week-old vs. 4-week-old, p=0.0179; Mann-Whitney test for post hoc analysis).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: Dopamine receptor mutant flies maintained their decreased general reactivity throughout all age groups.
source: Thus, different types of escape reactions showed remarkable tendencies across the fly lifespan, while dopamine receptor mutant flies maintained their decreased general reactivity throughout all age groups.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study's age-group comparison experiments.

claim: The lack of dopamine action through Dop1R may be one of the common pathways underlying motor deficits in Parkin flies.
source: We found similarities between Parkin and Dop1R mutant flies in their altered responses to predator-mimicking passing shadows: reduced walking speed and decreased overall reactivity, suggesting that the lack of dopamine action through Dop1R may be one of the common pathways underlying motor deficits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed similarities between Parkin and Dop1R mutant flies.

claim: Parkin flies should be favored as a genetic model of human Parkinson's disease over α-Synuclein flies, at least with respect to motor deficits.
source: The modest phenotype of A53T α-Syn compared to Parkin flies suggests that the latter should be favored as a genetic model of human PD, at least with respect to the motor deficits examined in this study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of behavioral phenotypes between Parkin and α-Syn flies.

claim: Single-trial behavioral analysis can reveal subtle behavioral changes in mutant flies.
source: Our data demonstrate that single-trial behavioral analysis can reveal subtle behavioral changes in mutant flies that can be used to further our understanding of disease pathomechanisms and help gauge the validity of genetic Drosophila models of neurodegeneration, taking us one step closer to bridging the gap in fly-to-human translation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The fruit fly central complex and vertebrate basal ganglia share homologies in motor control mediated by GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons.
source: Specifically, a deep-running evolutional conservation has been revealed between the arthropod central complex and the vertebrate basal ganglia, where GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons play key roles in motor control in both phyla (Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Clusters of fly dopaminergic neurons that project to the ellipsoid body, fan-shaped body, and lateral accessory lobes share homologies with striatum-projecting dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra in mammals.
source: Clusters of fly dopaminergic neurons that project to the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, and the lateral accessory lobes are thought to share homologies with the striatum-projecting dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about evolutionary homologies.

claim: Fruit flies lacking tyrosine hydroxylase enzyme in the central nervous system show reduced activity and locomotor deficit that worsen with age.
source: It has been found that fruit flies lacking the DA-synthesizing tyrosine hydroxylase enzyme in the central nervous system show reduced activity and locomotor deficit that worsen with age and also exhibit marked impairments in associative learning based on both appetitive and aversive reinforcement (Riemensperger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The dopaminergic nigrostriatal pathway plays a role in controlling goal-directed action in mammals.

claim: Age-related changes in motor behavior in response to threatening stimuli may parallel the age-dependent worsening of Parkinson's disease symptoms in humans.

evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the age-related findings.

claim: Looming stimuli and passing shadows can both be considered as threat-inducing visual stimuli.
source: We found the same escape behavioral repertoire as in studies with looming stimuli and ReVSA (Gibson et al., 2015; Zacarias et al., 2018), with a similar dependence on walking speed (Zacarias et al., 2018; Oram and Card, 2022), confirming that looming stimuli and passing shadows can both be considered as threat-inducing visual stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of behavioral responses to different stimuli types, supported by citations.

claim: The DopEcR may serve as an integrative hub for dopamine-mediated actions and stress responses in fruit flies.
source: It has been proposed that the DopEcR may serve as an integrative hub for dopamine-mediated actions and stress responses in fruit flies (Petruccelli et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The DopEcR may convey similar dopamine-mediated functions as DopR1 in motor aspects.
source: This pattern of alterations was largely similar to those observed in Parkin and Dop1R mutant flies, suggesting that the DopEcR may convey similar dopamine-mediated functions as DopR1, at least in those motor aspects tested in the present study.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Serotonin modulates both walking speed and startle response in flies.
source: A recent work demonstrated that serotonin also modulates both walking speed and startle response in flies, suggesting a complex neuromodulatory control over Drosophila motor behavior (Howard et al., 2019).

claim: The experimental arena allows simultaneous recording of the movement of animals and shadows.

claim: The experimental sessions consisted of 40 trials of 2-second-long shadow presentations separated by pseudorandom inter-trial intervals.
source: We recorded 40-min-long sessions, consisting of 40 trials of 2-s-long shadow presentations separated by pseudorandom inter-trial intervals to prevent the animals from learning temporal expectations of the shadow presentations (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Pseudorandom inter-trial intervals were used to prevent animals from learning temporal expectations of shadow presentations.

claim: Cluster boundaries in hierarchical clustering were sensitive to genotype-specific differences across groups of flies.

claim: Reactions were considered robust if the absolute value of acceleration reached 200 mm/s².
source: Reactions were considered robust if the absolute value of the acceleration reached 200 mm/s2; otherwise, the trial was classified as a 'no reaction' trial.
evidence: This describes a methodological criterion used in the study.

claim: Two-week-old Drosophila melanogaster (both males and females) were used for experiments presented in Figures 1-4.
source: We used 2-week-old Drosophila melanogaster (both males and females) raised at 24 °C and 60% humidity in a natural light-dark cycle for experiments presented in Figures 1—4.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and conditions.

claim: For age-group comparisons, fruit flies aged 1, 7, 14, 21, and 28 days were used and raised at 29°C and 70% humidity to accelerate aging.
source: For age-group comparisons (Figure 5), fruit flies aged 1, 7, 14, 21, and 28 days were used. These flies were raised at 29 °C and 70% humidity to accelerate aging.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and conditions for age-group studies.

claim: The arena was designed with tunnels that allowed individual flies to move freely in two dimensions but could not fly.
source: We designed an arena made of four layers of plexiglass and metal that formed 13 tunnels (Figure 1a). Each tunnel was 52 mm x 5 mm ×1.5 mm, in which individual flies were able to move freely in two dimensions but could not fly.
evidence: This describes the design and function of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The frame rate for tracking was set to 100 frames per second to allow detection of position with high temporal resolution.
source: The frame rate was set to 100 frames/second to allow the detection of position with high temporal resolution.
evidence: This describes a technical parameter of the experimental setup.

claim: Red color stimuli were perceived by fruit flies as dark shadows and enabled continuous tracking of the animals.
source: We implemented 'shadow' stimuli in red color, as these stimuli were suggested to be perceived by fruit flies as dark shadows and also enabled continuous tracking of the animals (Sharkey et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Shadow stimuli were separated by pseudorandomized inter-trial intervals with an approximately exponential distribution with a mean of 52.2 seconds.
source: The shadow stimuli were separated by pseudorandomized inter-trial intervals with an approximately exponential distribution with a mean of 52.2 s, preventing flies from anticipating the next shadow stimulus.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Principal component analysis was used to reduce dimensionality of normalized speed functions.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to reduce dimensionality of the normalized speed functions in the 1 s interval following shadow presentation in a way that the variance between trials is maximally preserved in the low-dimensional representation.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method used.

claim: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering was performed in the space spanned by the first three principal components to identify trials with distinct characteristic response types.
